summary: This document specifies a method to find which Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) server is authoritative for a requested scope, such as domain names, IP addresses, or Autonomous System numbers. It was replaced by RFC 9224.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a program can look up who owns a domain name or an IP address, it has to know which server holds that record. This RFC says how: IANA publishes a small JSON list of scopes and their servers, and the program looks up the scope in that list before making its query.

questions: how to find the right rdap server
what is the rdap bootstrap service
how does rdap domain longest match work
what format are the iana rdap bootstrap registries
subtitle: How an RDAP client works out which registry server to ask, using JSON bootstrap files published by IANA.

tldr.problem: RDAP says how to query registration data, but not where to send the query. The server that answers depends on whether the name is a domain, an IP address or an autonomous system number, and on which registry holds it.
tldr.mechanism: IANA publishes a bootstrap registry as JSON for each of the four scopes. The client fetches the registry, matches the query against its entries, and takes the base URL of the longest matching entry, then appends the query path defined for that object type.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7484 was a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9224 and updated by RFC 8521.

sections.title: The Missing Piece: Where to Send the Query
sections.content:
Querying and retrieving registration data from registries is defined in the Registration Data Access Protocol documents. Those documents do not specify where to send the queries. This document specifies a method to find which server is authoritative to answer queries for the requested scope.

The reason this can be built from existing data is a matter of how allocation works. Top-Level Domains, Autonomous System numbers and network blocks are delegated by IANA to Internet registries such as TLD registries and Regional Internet Registries, which then issue further delegations and maintain information about them. The bootstrap information needed by RDAP clients is therefore best generated from data and processes already maintained by IANA, and the relevant registries already exist for IPv4 addresses, IPv6 addresses, AS numbers and domain names.

Per this document, IANA has created new registries based on a JSON format specified in it, named RDAP Bootstrap Service Registries. These new registries are based on the existing entries of the allocation registries. An RDAP client fetches the RDAP Bootstrap Service Registries, extracts the data, and then performs a match with the query data to find the authoritative registration data server and the appropriate query base URL.
sections.plainLanguage: The allocation registries already know which organisation holds which block of names or addresses. The bootstrap registries reuse that, adding one thing: the web address of the server that answers for it.

sections.title: The Structure of the Bootstrap Registries
sections.content:
The registries are JSON objects that can be retrieved over HTTP from locations specified by IANA. The JSON object for each registry contains members giving metadata about it: a version identifier, a timestamp of the publication date, and a description. A services member holds the registry items themselves as an array.

Each item of that array is a second-level array with two elements, in order an Entry Array and a Service URL Array. The Entry Array contains all entries that have the same set of base RDAP URLs. The Service URL Array contains the list of base RDAP URLs usable for the entries found in the Entry Array. Elements within these two arrays are not sorted in any way.

The version member corresponds to the format version of the registry, and this specification defines version 1.0. The syntax of the publication value conforms to the Internet date and time format of RFC 3339, and its value is the latest update date of the registry by IANA. The optional description string can carry a comment about the content of the bootstrap object.

Three rules govern the URLs and the names. Per RFC 7258, in each array of base RDAP URLs the secure versions of the transport protocol should be preferred and tried first, so if the array holds both HTTPS and HTTP URLs the client should try the HTTPS version first. Base RDAP URLs must have a trailing "/" character, because they are concatenated to the various segments defined in RFC 7482. Any unrecognized JSON object properties or values must be ignored by implementations.

Two rules govern the domain labels. Internationalized Domain Name labels used as entries or base RDAP URLs must be represented only using their A-label form as defined in RFC 5890. All Domain Name labels used as entries or base RDAP URLs must be represented only in lowercase.
sections.plainLanguage: The file is a list of pairs: a group of names or prefixes, and the server addresses that answer for them. Nothing in it is sorted, so the client has to search it itself.

sections.title: Finding the Server for a Domain Name
sections.content:
The domain name's authoritative registration data service is found by doing the label-wise longest match of the target domain name with the domain values in the Entry Arrays of the IANA Bootstrap Service Registry for Domain Name Space. The match is done per label, from right to left. If the longest match results in multiple entries, those entries are considered equivalent. The values contained in the Service URL Array of the matching second-level array are the valid base RDAP URLs.

The RFC's example is concrete. A domain RDAP query for a.b.example.com matches the com entry in one of the arrays of the registry. The base RDAP URL is then taken from the second element of that array, which is the only one available in the example, https://registry.example.com/myrdap/. The segment specified in RFC 7482 is appended to the base URL to complete the query, giving https://registry.example.com/myrdap/domain/a.b.example.com.

Two refinements follow. If a query for a.b.example.com matches both a com entry and an example.com entry, the longest match applies and the example.com entry is used. And if the registry contains entries such as com and goodexample.com, a query for example.com matches only the com entry, because matching is done on a per-label basis. The entry for the root of the domain name space is specified as the empty string.

Entities, such as contacts, registrants or registrars, can be queried by handle as described in RFC 7482. Because there is no global namespace for entities, this document does not describe how to find the authoritative RDAP server for them. It is possible, however, that if the entity identifier was received from a previous query, the same RDAP server could be queried, or the entity identifier itself is a fully referenced URL that can be queried.
sections.plainLanguage: Domain names are matched label by label, starting from the right, and the closest match wins. That stops a registry entry for a domain that merely looks similar from catching the wrong name.

sections.title: Finding the Server for IP Addresses and AS Numbers
sections.content:
For IP address space, the authoritative registration data service is found by doing a longest match of the target address with the values of the arrays in the corresponding registry. The longest match is done the same way as for routing: the addresses are converted in binary form and then the binary strings are compared to find the longest match up to the specified prefix length. The longest match method enables covering prefixes of a larger address space pointing to one base RDAP URL while more specific prefixes within the covering prefix are served by another base RDAP URL.

The IPv4 registry holds entries in Classless Inter-domain Routing format. In the RFC's example, a query for 192.0.2.1/25 matches the 192.0.0.0/8 entry and the 192.0.2.0/24 entry, and the latter is chosen by the client given the longest match. The IPv6 registry holds entries in the text representation of RFC 4291. A query for 2001:0200:1000::/48 matches the 2001:0200::/23 entry and the 2001:0200:1000::/36 entry, and the latter is chosen. The client picks the secure version of the protocol when the array offers both, giving the complete query https://example.net/rdaprir2/ip/2001:0200:1000::/48. If the target RDAP server does not answer, the client can then use another URL prefix from the array.

The AS number registry holds ranges. The Entry Array contains the list of AS number ranges served by the base RDAP URLs, and the array always contains two AS numbers in decimal format that represent the range between the two elements. A single AS number is represented as a range of two identical AS numbers. In the example, a query for AS 65411 matches the 64512-65534 entry, and the complete query is https://example.net/rdaprir2/autnum/65411.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses are matched the same way routers match them: the most specific prefix wins. A block inside a larger block can point at a different server.

sections.title: Deployment, Caching and Limits
sections.content:
The method relies on clients fetching the IANA registries and then finding the servers locally. Clients should not fetch the registry on every RDAP request. They should cache the registry, but use underlying protocol signalling, such as the HTTP Expires header field, to identify when it is time to refresh the cached registry.

When the query data does not match any entry in the cached registry, the client has options. For a domain object it may first query the DNS to see whether the entry has been delegated or the user mistyped it, for example by fetching the NS records for the TLD domain. A negative DNS answer means there is no need to fetch a new version of the registry; a positive one may mean the cached registry is no longer current, so the client can fetch, parse and match as normal. Alternatively, if the client knows the existence of an RDAP aggregator or redirector and its base URL, and trusts that service, it could send the query to the redirector, which would redirect the client if it knows the authoritative server the client has not found.

The RFC is candid about gaps. When a new object is allocated, such as a new AS range, a new TLD or a new IP address range, there is no guarantee that it will have an entry in the corresponding bootstrap registry, because the setup of the RDAP server may become live and registered later. Clients should expect that even if an object is allocated, the existence of the entry is not guaranteed. The registries may also not contain a requested value at all, in which case there is no known RDAP server and the client should provide an appropriate error message to the user.

The limitations are listed. This method does not provide a direct way to find authoritative RDAP servers for any objects other than the ones described. In particular it does not bootstrap entities, queries using search patterns that do not contain a terminating string that matches some entries in the registries, nameservers, or help.
sections.plainLanguage: The client keeps a copy of the list and refreshes it when IANA says it has changed. New allocations can take time to appear, and a few kinds of query are not covered by the list at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
By providing a bootstrap method to find RDAP servers, this document helps to ensure that end users get the RDAP data from an authoritative source, instead of from rogue sources. The method has the same security properties as the RDAP protocols themselves. The transport used to access the registries can be more secure by using TLS, which IANA supports. Additional considerations on using RDAP are described in RFC 7481.

The IANA section adds two operational details. Because these registries will be accessed by software, the download demand may be unusually high compared with normal IANA registries, so the technical infrastructure by which registries are published may need to be reviewed and augmented. And because software accessing these registries will depend on the HTTP Expires header field to limit its query rate, it is important for that header field to be properly set to provide timely information as the registries change, while maintaining a reasonable load on the IANA servers. The HTTP Content-Type returned to clients accessing these JSON-formatted registries must be application/json.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the bootstrap list is that a client reaches the real registry instead of a look-alike. The list itself is fetched over TLS.
